'''François Gros''' ({{IPA|fr|fʁɑ̃swa ɡʁo}}; 24 April 1925 – 18 February 2022) was a French biologist and one of the pioneers of cellular biochemistry in France. His scientific career concerned genes and their role in regulating cellular functions.<ref name="AdS">{{Cite web|lang=fr|title=François Gros - Membre de l'Académie des sciences|trans-title=François Gros - Member of the French Academy of Sciences|url=http://www.academie-sciences.fr/pdf/membre/GrosF_bio160311.pdf|website=French Academy of Sciences|access-date=19 October 2018}}</ref>

==Career==
François Gros studied at the Faculty of Science of the [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]]. Previously he had enrolled in error (see below: Personal life) at the Faculty of Sciences in [[University of Toulouse|Toulouse]]. After a junior position at the [[CNRS]] he was awarded a [[Rockefeller grant]] to study in the laboratory of microbiology of the [[University of Illinois]] and in the [[Rockefeller University|Rockefeller Institute]]. He entered the CNRS in 1957 as Maître de Recherche and later as Directeur de Recherche.<ref name="CdF"/>

In 1968 he became Professor in the Faculty of Science in Paris, where he became Chair of the Microbiology Department. In 1972 he became Professor at the [[Institut Pasteur]], head of biochemistry. In parallel he was Professor at the  [[Collège de France]] as Chair of cellular biochemistry.<ref name="CdF"/>

Honorary professor at the [[Collège de France]], member of the [[Institute of France]], and also director of the [[Pasteur Institute]] from 1976 to 1982.<ref name="CdF">{{Cite web|lang=fr|title=Biographie|trans-title=Biography|url=http://www.college-de-france.fr/site/francois-gros/index.htm|website=College de France|access-date=19 October 2018}}</ref> In this last capacity during 1981 to 1985 he acted as advisor to two Prime Ministers, [[Pierre Mauroy]] and [[Laurent Fabius]].<ref name="Papon">{{Cite web|lang=fr|title=Entretien avec Pierre Papon|trans-title=Interview with Pierre Papon|url=http://www.histcnrs.fr/archives-orales/papon.html|website=History of the CNRS|date=9 May 1988|access-date=19 October 2018}}</ref> Partially as a consequence of this he became involved in the health scandal of contaminated blood ([[:fr:Affaire du sang contaminé]]) when many haemophilia patients were transfused with blood containing [[HIV]].

==Honours==
Elected correspondent (1977) then member (1979) of the [[French Academy of Sciences]], he was permanent secretary from 1991 to 2000.<ref name="AdS"/>

==Personal life==
François Gros was born in Paris on 24th April 1925, son of Alexandre Gros and Yvonne Pauline née Haguenauer, from a secular Jewish family. During the Second World War he fled first to [[Brive]] and then took refuge in Toulouse, changing names several times. Although he was planning to study medicine, he mistakenly enrolled at the Faculty of Sciences in Toulouse to study botany before moving to Paris and the Sorbonne.<ref>{{cite journal |title = François Gros (1925–2022), Co-discoverer of messenger RNA who advanced French life sciences|author = Georgina Ferry|journal = Nature|url=  https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-022-00794-0|year = 2022|volume = 603|pages = 573
|doi= 10.1038/d41586-022-00794-0|url-access = subscription}}</ref>

He died at the age of 96, also in Paris, on the 18th February 2022.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.elysee.fr/emmanuel-macron/2022/02/21/deces-du-professeur-francois-gros|title = Décès du professeur François Gros}}</ref><ref>[https://www.nouvelobs.com/sciences/20220220.OBS54740/le-biologiste-francois-gros-codecouvreur-de-l-arn-messager-est-mort.html Le biologiste François Gros, codécouvreur de l’ARN messager, est mort] {{in lang|fr}}</ref> He was married with three children.
